title: Industrialization and imperialism
note: Beginning in Britain around 1760, machines powered by water, steam and coal moved work from homes into factories. Industry made Western states rich and militarily powerful, and from the 1870s they used that power to seize colonies across Africa and Asia in what historians call the New Imperialism.

read.title: Machines and empires
text: In the mid-1700s, Britain had coal and iron, capital from trade, growing markets in its colonies, and workers pushed off the land by enclosure. Inventors built machines to spin and weave cotton, and James Watt's improved steam engine let factories run anywhere. Railways and steamships followed. Output soared, but early factory life was harsh: long hours, child labor and crowded cities. Reformers won laws limiting work hours, workers formed unions, and Karl Marx called for a revolution against capitalism.

After 1870 a second wave of industry brought cheap steel, electricity and chemicals, and it spread to Germany, the United States and Japan. Industrial nations wanted raw materials such as rubber and cotton, new markets, naval bases and national prestige. Social Darwinism offered a false scientific excuse, claiming some peoples were fit to rule others. New tools made conquest easier: quinine protected Europeans from malaria, steamboats carried them up rivers, and machine guns overwhelmed armies.

At the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885, European powers set rules for dividing Africa without any African present. By 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent. In Asia, Britain ruled India directly after 1858 and forced China open in the Opium Wars, while Japan avoided colonization by modernizing quickly after the Meiji Restoration.
